strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically relevant problem: neural multi-objective routing on multigraphs, which as far as the related work indicates has not been tackled before with learning-based methods for combinatorial problems like TSP/VRP.

Two well-motivated architectural variants (edge-based GMS-EB and dual-head GMS-DH) offer a sensible trade-off between simplicity/accuracy and scalability/speed, and the design choices (hypernetwork preference conditioning, GREAT encoder, multi-pointer decoder, curriculum learning) are grounded in established techniques adapted thoughtfully to the multigraph setting.

Theoretical grounding via Proposition 1 clarifies when pruning is exact under linear scalarization, motivating why a learned selection mechanism is needed for more general cases (e.g., Chebyshev scalarization or nonlinear costs like time-windows).

Extensive experimental evaluation across many problem types (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOTSPTW), distributions (EUC, TMAT, XASY, FIX, FLEX), instance sizes, and baselines (LKH, OR-tools, four MOEAs, a custom MatNet-based neural baseline), with substantial appendix material including ablations and zero-shot generalization to larger instances/more edges.

Informative ablation studies (GMS-DH vs. pre-pruning variant, learned vs. simple pruning) that isolate the contribution of the learned edge-selection mechanism, particularly showing its value in the more complex time-window setting.
Reports both solution quality (HV) and runtime, offering a fairly complete picture of the accuracy/speed trade-offs relative to strong non-learning baselines like LKH3.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily architectural recombination of existing components (GREAT encoder, POMO, MatNet, multi-pointer decoder, hypernetwork conditioning) applied to a new problem setting, rather than fundamentally new algorithmic ideas; the core technical contribution is somewhat incremental.

All experiments rely on synthetic distributions (FIX/FLEX, TMAT/XASY) for multigraph edges; despite the paper's motivation citing real-world VRP cost savings from multigraph modeling, there is no evaluation on real or semi-realistic multigraph network data (e.g., actual road networks with alternative paths), leaving practical relevance somewhat unvalidated.

On the core MOTSP and MGMOTSP benchmarks, the proposed models do not outperform the strong classical heuristic LKH3 in solution quality (only closing most of the gap), so the main benefit is speed rather than better solutions; this weakens the 'competitive results' claim in some settings, especially as LKH is not really a learning baseline competitor in the traditional sense.

GMS-EB scales poorly (O(MN^4)) and has very high training times (e.g., 1.7h/epoch on multigraphs), which raises reproducibility/practicality concerns, particularly given 200 training epochs and multiple problem/distribution combinations evaluated.

The paper does not empirically compare against recently cited neural methods for asymmetric-graph MO routing (Santiyuda et al. 2024; Zhou, Kong, and Wang 2025), even in adapted/simplified form, which would have strengthened claims of relative performance.

The multigraph distributions considered (FIX2/FLEX2, occasionally FIX5/FLEX5) involve a small, fixed number of parallel edges, which may not capture the complexity or heterogeneity of real multigraph scenarios (e.g., many alternative routes with correlated attributes).

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored problem setting: multi-objective routing on multigraphs, for which the authors claim (plausibly) the first neural solvers.

Two complementary architectures (edge-based GMS-EB and dual-head GMS-DH) are proposed with a clear speed/simplicity trade-off, and the authors provide a reasonable complexity analysis (O(MN^4) vs node-based scaling).

Extensive experimental evaluation across several problems (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOTSPTW), multiple distributions (EUC, TMAT, XASY, FIXx, FLEXx), and instance sizes, compared against a fairly broad set of baselines (LKH, OR-Tools, four MOEAs, a custom MatNet-based neural baseline).
Includes informative ablations (GMS-DH with pre-pruning vs. learned selection vs. simple linear pruning) that help isolate the contribution of the learned edge-selection component.
Zero-shot generalization experiments to larger instances and higher numbers of parallel edges add some evidence of robustness.
Proposition 1 gives a clean theoretical grounding for when multigraph pruning is lossless under linear scalarization, motivating the architectural choices.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the approach is largely a recombination of existing components (GREAT encoder, MatNet, Multi-Pointer decoder, hypernetwork preference-conditioning from Navon et al./Lin et al., POMO rollouts, Chebyshev/linear scalarization), with the multigraph-specific additions (edge-based decoding, selection-decoder) being relatively incremental engineering extensions rather than a conceptual advance.

Despite being the paper's main motivation, the proposed methods generally underperform the strong classical single-objective solver LKH (combined with scalarization) across MOTSP and MGMOTSP; gains are mainly over weaker neural baselines (MBM) and MOEAs, which somewhat undercuts the claimed practical value of the neural approach for these settings.

The multigraph distributions used for evaluation (FIXx, FLEXx) are synthetic and arbitrarily constructed (sorting/dominance-based edge generation) rather than derived from or validated against real-world multigraph routing data (e.g., actual road networks with multiple alternative paths), despite the paper's motivation being grounded in real-world logistics applications (Ben Ticha et al., Capgemini report).
No real-world case study or dataset is used to demonstrate practical impact, which is a significant gap given the paper's framing around real-world relevance of multigraph routing.

Evaluation is restricted to bi-objective (m=2) problems even though the formulation and motivation emphasize general multi-objective settings (m>1); it is unclear how well the approach scales to 3+ objectives.

GMS-EB has very poor training scalability (up to 1.7h/epoch on multigraph problems, Table 4) and its decoding complexity (O(MN^4)) raises concerns about practicality for larger graphs or higher edge multiplicities beyond what was tested.

The MGMOTSPTW experiments, which are presented as the most realistic/motivating multigraph case, are only evaluated on very small instances (20 and 50 nodes), limiting the evidence that gains persist at practically relevant scales.

Missing direct comparison/adaptation of the most closely related existing asymmetric neural routing methods (Santiyuda et al. 2024; Zhou, Kong, and Wang 2025), even though they are discussed as the only other learning-based approaches for asymmetric graphs; the justification that they are 'problem-specific' is not fully substantiated with an attempted adaptation or qualitative comparison.
Proposition 1 is stated as trivial by the authors, offering limited additional theoretical insight beyond motivating the pruning baseline.

strengths: Novel and practically motivated problem formulation: the paper is the first to address multi-objective routing on multigraphs with neural methods, a setting with clear real-world relevance (e.g., last-mile delivery, VRPTW) that prior neural routing work has ignored.

Two well-motivated architectures (edge-based GMS-EB and dual-head GMS-DH) with a clear trade-off analysis between simplicity/accuracy and scalability/speed, built on a sensible combination of GREAT encoders, hypernetwork preference-conditioning, and multi-pointer decoding.

Theoretical grounding via Proposition 1 clarifying when multigraph pruning preserves optimality under linear scalarization, and the paper correctly identifies and empirically demonstrates when this pruning breaks down (Chebyshev scalarization, MGMOTSPTW).

Extensive and carefully designed experimental evaluation: multiple problems (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOTSPTW), multiple distributions (EUC, TMAT, XASY, FLEX/FIX), multiple instance sizes, strong classical baselines (LKH, OR-Tools, four MOEAs), a custom neural baseline (MBM) built from MatNet, and thorough ablations (pre-pruning vs. learned selection, simple vs. learned pruning) plus zero-shot generalization tests.

Good transparency regarding limitations and trade-offs (e.g., GMS-EB's poor scaling O(MN^4), GMS-DH's loss of context-dependence in edge selection) and honest discussion of cases where the proposed methods underperform (e.g., GMS-DH PP producing poor-diversity fronts).

Appendices provide substantial additional detail (architecture formulas, training curricula, MOEA implementation details, extended results), supporting reproducibility despite code not yet being released.
weaknesses: On the core MOTSP and MGMOTSP benchmarks, the proposed methods generally do not outperform LKH in solution quality (only closing most of the gap), so the main advantage demonstrated is inference speed rather than solution quality; the strongest quality gains appear mainly on MOCVRP.

Multigraph distributions (FLEXx/FIXx) are synthetic and do not derive from real road-network data, which is at odds with the paper's motivating real-world applications (e.g., Ben Ticha et al., Capgemini last-mile statistics); no validation on realistic multigraph instances is provided.

Only bi-objective variants are studied; it is unclear how the proposed hypernetwork/Chebyshev-reward framework scales to more than two objectives, which is a common limitation of Pareto-front learning methods but is not discussed or tested.

The core architectural components (GREAT encoder, MatNet, hypernetwork preference conditioning, POMO-style rollouts, multi-pointer decoder) are all adopted from prior work; the technical novelty largely lies in combining/adapting these for multigraph edge selection rather than introducing fundamentally new mechanisms.

The MatNet-based baseline (MBM) requires pre-pruning for multigraphs and is explicitly described as an 'off-the-shelf' combination rather than a carefully optimized competitor, which may make comparisons against it less informative about the true difficulty of the baseline approach.

Runtime comparisons between GPU-based neural methods and CPU-based classical heuristics/MOEAs, while reasonably justified, still involve different hardware classes and parallelization choices that complicate direct efficiency conclusions.
Code is not yet released (promised only upon acceptance), limiting independent verification of the fairly complex training procedures (dual-head REINFORCE, curriculum learning) at submission time.

strengths: Addresses a novel and practically motivated problem (multi-objective routing on multigraphs) that has not been tackled by neural methods before, clearly differentiating this work from prior neural CO literature that assumes simple graphs.

Proposes two complementary architectures (GMS-EB and GMS-DH) with a clear trade-off between simplicity/accuracy and scalability, both built on a principled GNN encoder (GREAT) adapted for edge-permutation invariance in multigraphs.

Extensive empirical evaluation across many problem variants (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOCVRP, MGMOTSPTW), distributions (EUC, TMAT, XASY, FLEX, FIX), instance sizes, and objective counts (bi- and tri-objective), with strong classical baselines (LKH, HGS, OR-tools) and multiple MOEAs.

Careful ablation studies (e.g., GMS-DH with pre-pruning vs. learned selection-decoder, and simplified pruning heuristic vs. learned pruning) that isolate the contribution of the proposed learned edge-selection mechanism, particularly convincing on the harder MGMOTSPTW problem.

Thoughtful theoretical grounding (Proposition 1) explaining when simple pruning suffices and motivating why learned pruning is needed in more general (e.g., nonlinear or Chebyshev-scalarized) settings.

Thorough appendix work, including additional naive neural baselines (GRBM, GOBM) that show the proposed method's robustness is not merely an artifact of using a particular baseline, plus zero-shot generalization experiments to larger sizes and more parallel edges.
weaknesses: GMS-EB has poor scaling (O(MN^4)) and very long training times (e.g., 1.7h/epoch on multigraphs per Table 4), which limits its practical applicability despite being presented as a core contribution.

The multigraph distributions (FLEXx, FIXx) are synthetic constructions for benchmarking purposes and do not obey the triangle inequality or reflect realistic transportation network structure; no experiments are conducted on real-world or more realistic multigraph instances (e.g., derived from actual road networks as in Ben Ticha et al.), leaving the practical relevance claims not fully substantiated empirically.

On several core problems (MOTSP, MGMOTSP, MGMOCVRP) the proposed neural methods do not outperform strong classical solvers like LKH/HGS/OR-tools, only closing part of the gap, which somewhat tempers the significance of the contribution relative to non-learning approaches, though this is a common characteristic of neural CO work.

Several architectural components (GREAT encoder, multi-pointer decoder, hypernetwork preference conditioning) are directly reused or lightly adapted from prior work, so the core novelty lies primarily in combining these pieces for the multigraph setting and in the selection-decoder design, which is a relatively incremental (albeit well-executed) contribution.

GMS-DH's zero-shot performance degrades noticeably for larger numbers of parallel edges (e.g., FIX10-100), suggesting the learned selection-decoder does not scale robustly with edge multiplicity, a limitation acknowledged but not deeply analyzed.

The paper's presentation relies heavily on extensive appendices (novelty justification, architecture details, extended related work) to substantiate claims made in the main text, suggesting the main paper alone may not fully convey the technical contribution and comparisons clearly.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely novel and underexplored problem setting: neural MO routing specifically designed for multigraphs, which to the authors' knowledge has not been tackled before by any learning-based method.

Two architecturally distinct solutions (GMS-EB, GMS-DH) are proposed with clear complexity trade-offs (O(MN^4) edge-based vs O(N^3) node-based with learned pruning), and the paper is transparent about the scaling weaknesses of each.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: multiple problems (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOCVRP, MGMOTSPTW), multiple distributions (TMAT, XASY, FLEX, FIX), multiple sizes, zero-shot generalization, tri-objective extensions, and several ablations (pre-pruning variant, simple-pruning variant, additional naive neural baselines GRBM/GOBM/CNH).
Includes a small theoretical result (Proposition 1) connecting linear scalarization to graph pruning, which motivates and contextualizes the architectural design.

Honest reporting: the paper does not hide cases where classical heuristics (LKH, HGS) or the MatNet baseline outperform the proposed methods, and discusses failure modes (e.g., GMS-DH PP producing poorly diverse fronts).
weaknesses: Despite the paper's motivation emphasizing real-world relevance of multigraphs (citing VRPTW studies with reported 5-10% real-world savings), all multigraph experiments use synthetic FIX/FLEX distributions with no real-world or semi-realistic benchmark instances, leaving the practical significance of the proposed methods largely unvalidated.

The actual performance gains are often modest: LKH/HGS with simple linear-scalarization pruning still outperform both GMS variants in a majority of MOTSP/MGMOTSP/MGMOCVRP settings, and GMS methods typically trail the best non-neural baseline by 1-5% HV gap, raising questions about the practical value added by the more complex multigraph-aware architecture versus simply scalarizing and pruning with strong classical solvers.
GMS-EB has very poor training scalability (up to 1.7h/epoch on multigraphs, per Table 4), which is a substantial practical limitation not fully mitigated by the curriculum-learning workaround.

The paper omits direct comparison to the operations-research multigraph heuristics it cites as motivation (e.g., tabu search of Lai et al., ALNS of Ben Ticha et al.), so it is unclear how GMS compares to the actual state of the art for multigraph VRPs in the OR literature, only to naive neural/evolutionary baselines and generic solvers applied to linearly-pruned graphs.

The architecture stacks many specialized components (GREAT encoder, hypernetwork conditioning, dual decoders, selection-decoder, curriculum learning, POMO augmentation) with limited isolated ablation of each piece's individual contribution beyond the pruning-head ablation, making it hard to assess which design choices actually drive the reported gains.

The MGMOTSPTW experiment, the one case argued to be genuinely difficult for simple pruning, is only evaluated at N=50, which is a fairly narrow validation of the core motivating claim (that learned, context-dependent edge pruning is necessary) for more complex objectives.

Writing and presentation are dense and require substantial appendix cross-referencing to follow the architecture and training details, which may limit accessibility and reproducibility, despite some of the content (e.g., full novelty justification) being pushed into appendices rather than being concisely argued in the main text.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely novel and practically motivated problem: neural routing on multigraphs, which existing methods cannot handle. The paper clearly articulates why simple-graph pruning/transformation approaches are insufficient (Appendix B).

Proposes two complementary architectures (GMS-EB, edge-based, and GMS-DH, dual-head NAR+AR) with a sensible accuracy/scalability trade-off, built on a principled GREAT encoder adapted for edge-permutation-invariant multigraph inputs.

Very extensive experimental evaluation: multiple problems (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOCVRP, MGMOTSPTW), multiple distributions (EUC/TMAT/XASY, FLEX/FIX), instance sizes, zero-shot generalization to larger graphs/more parallel edges, and tri-objective extensions.

Strong and diverse baselines, including classical solvers (LKH, HGS, OR-tools), MOEAs, and carefully constructed neural baselines (MBM, GRBM, GOBM) that demonstrate naive extensions of existing single-objective/asymmetric solvers fail to generalize robustly, strengthening the case for the proposed design.

Thoughtful ablations (GMS-DH with pre-pruning, GMS-DH with simple linear pruning vs learned pruning) that isolate the benefit of the proposed multigraph-aware architecture and learned edge-selection mechanism, including a harder problem (MGMOTSPTW) where simple pruning fails but learned pruning succeeds.

Reasonable theoretical grounding (Proposition 1 on linear scalarization and pruning) used to motivate and contextualize the architectural choices and their limits (e.g., under Chebyshev scalarization).
Good transparency about limitations (e.g., GMS-EB's poor scaling, long training times) and honest reporting of cases where GMS underperforms (e.g., tri-objective XASY100 for GMS-DH).
weaknesses: All experiments are on synthetic distributions (FLEX/FIX edge sampling); there is no evaluation on real-world or realistic multigraph road-network data, which is the primary motivation given in the introduction (citing 5-10% real-world savings from OR literature) but never directly validated.

On the core MOTSP/MGMOTSP problems, GMS does not outperform strong classical solvers (LKH) in solution quality; the main advantage is speed. This is a reasonable trade-off but should be more explicitly framed as the central contribution rather than general 'competitive performance.'

GMS-EB has poor scaling (O(MN^4) decoding) and very long training times (up to ~1.7h/epoch for 50-node multigraphs), raising questions about practicality for larger M or N despite the curriculum learning mitigation.

The paper is very dense with many interacting components (dual decoders, hypernetworks, Chebyshev/linear rewards, curriculum learning, pruning variants), which may hinder reproducibility and clarity despite the detailed appendices.

The FIX/FLEX synthetic distributions used for multigraph edges may not reflect realistic correlations between objectives (e.g., travel time and distance are typically correlated in practice, unlike the independent/anti-correlated sampling used here), limiting external validity of the multigraph-specific results.

GMS-DH's selection-decoder performance appears to degrade with more parallel edges (e.g., FIX10-100 zero-shot), suggesting potential scalability limits of the learned pruning approach that are only partially explored.
